newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain electric firms eye pending regulatory regime.
newsitem.headline: Spain electric firms eye pending regulatory regime.

text.p: Spain's electricity firms are due to report an average 15 percent rise in nine-month earnings in the next fortnight, but the breakdown of results, particularly at year-end, will depend on the new tariff regime.

"Results all depend on what the tariff is, and how final (P&L) accounts are adjusted. Firms are likely to adjust in the fourth quarter either to hide or to highlight earnings, depending on those changes," said Societe Generale Madrid's utilities analyst Alberto Nunez.

The government is currently in talks with major electricity firms to agree basic guidelines for a new regulatory framework, replacing the current system which compensates firms for the cost of their fixed assets through the tariff.
Industry Minister Josep Pique has said that the agreed protocol will likely be finalised during November.

Sixty-six percent state-owned Endesa last week announced an 11.8 percent rise in group attributable profit to 120.86 billion pesetas ($947.8 million) for the first nine months of the year. Other major companies are due to report earnings for the same period before November 15.

"The new (regulatory) framework is still very much on the table, and for that reason it is difficult to predict year-end profits growth. Two things which are important are how sunk costs are valued and over how much time they can be recouped, and how competition is set out, if total or partial," Nunez said.

For the nine months to end-September, Societe Generale forecasts a 24 pct rise in Sevillana's earnings to 18.2 bln ptas, Iberdrola results are seen up 19 pct to 76.13 bln ptas, Fecsa should increase 7 pct to 12.7 bln ptas and Fenosa is estimated to rise 36 pct to 16.8 bln ptas.
These highly-geared firms, particularly Fenosa, have benefited from lower lending rates this year, Nunez explained.

A London-based analyst said he was expecting nine-month results to show an average increase of 11-15 percent although he agreed that results could vary widely depending on the progress made in changing legislation governing the sector.
"It depends on how much competition there is, when it is introduced in distribution and generation, how much compensation the firms are given, and the ranking of different energy sources," he said.
Firms will have to be cautious on how they present results given public anger at what is seen as excessive earnings, part of the reason behind cuts in tariffs next year, he argued.
This would likely lead them to obscure earnings growth this year, shoring up accounts for subsequent years when the market will be more competitive and tariffs even lower, he argued.

In a November research note, brokerage BBV Interactivos said next year's three percent average electricity tariff reduction should not adversely affect quoted companies, although those weighted towards generation would be the most affected.

Amid uncertainty over the specifics of the new regime, BBV recommended Sevillana and Iberdrola who are less weighted in generation and, "due to financial and operating improvements are writing down debt more quickly."
